To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the policy problem of Schiphol expansion is not as intractable as it appears to be.

The Dutch government's approach to airport expansion is based on a narrow set of assumptions and policy alternatives that have led to a polarized and unproductive policy debate; and The Dutch policy debate on airport expansion has become polarized because of the government's narrow approach to the issue and its unwillingness to consider alternatives to airport expansion.

the Schiphol controversy can be recast by (1) redefining the policy problem to include a wider range of stakeholders and their policy arguments, (2) identifying the key policy arguments and the underlying policy values, and (3) using the key policy arguments to identify a new set of policy alternatives that move beyond polarization and allow the policy problem to be reexamined in a more tractable fashion.

we have shown that the use of Q methodology in a public policy context can be useful in the following ways: 1) It can be used to analyze the arguments of stakeholders in policy controversies; 2) It can be a tool for recasting intractability; and 3) It can be an important part of the policy analysis process.
The main takeaway from our work is that

recasting intractability requires a shift in the policy analysis paradigm from a focus on the policy process and the policy system to a more holistic approach that encompasses the wider context of policy making, including the policy environment, the policy issue, and the stakeholders' policy arguments.
the method we have used to recast the airport issue in The Netherlands can be used to recast any issue.
the method of recasting intractability is not only useful for the specific policy problem of airport expansion but also for a wide range of policy issues.
